title: Where did the swallows go, and why did the robin stay?
summary: An autumn sky empty of swallows leads to the question of why some birds fly thousands of miles to Africa while the robin stays for Christmas — and ends on the idea that each bird can only live the life its body is shaped for.
setting: An autumn afternoon, looking up at telephone wires where the swallows used to gather but are now gone.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: Where have all the swallows gone? They sat on these wires all summer.

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: They've flown south. All the way to Africa.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: To AFRICA? Why would they go that far?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: Because of what they eat. Swallows catch tiny insects in the air as they fly. When our winter comes, the flying insects vanish. So the swallows chase the summer — and when it's winter here, it's warm and full of insects down there.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: But the robin's still here, Grandad. I can hear it. Why didn't the robin go to Africa as well?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: The robin eats different food — worms, beetles, berries, whatever it can find down on the ground. There's still some of that around in our winter. The robin can stay and make do.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: Is THAT why robins are on Christmas cards and swallows aren't?

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: That's exactly why. The robin is the little bird that keeps us company right through the cold.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: But if staying works fine for the robin... why doesn't the swallow just learn to eat worms and stay too? Then it wouldn't have to fly so far.

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: Ah. Look at how a swallow is built. Long, narrow wings made for swooping. A wide mouth for scooping insects out of the air. And feet so tiny it can barely shuffle along the ground.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: So it couldn't dig up a worm even if it wanted to.

turns.speaker: adult
turns.text: It couldn't. Every bird can only really live the life its body is shaped for. The swallow's whole body says: follow the insects. So it does — across deserts, across a whole sea, across half the world — and then it finds its way back to the very same wire, next spring.

the_heart_of_it: Migration is driven by food, not simply by temperature: swallows leave because the flying insects they depend on disappear in a British winter, while robins, being ground-feeding generalists, can stay. The closing point — that a swallow can't simply choose to live like a robin because its body is specialised for aerial feeding — is an accessible first encounter with adaptation: form fits the way of life, which is why it foreshadows evolution (Y6) without naming it.
watch_for: Keep the cause as 'the food disappears', not 'it gets cold' — that's the accurate and more interesting reason. Swallows are insectivores that feed on the wing; robins are opportunist ground feeders. The remarkable fidelity of swallows returning to the same nest site is true and worth keeping for wonder.
extend_it: How does a young swallow, on its very first journey, know the way to Africa and back?
Which birds in our garden stay all winter, and which disappear? Keep a list across the year.
Compare the swallow's wings and feet with the robin's — draw both and label what each is good for.
